paras: The shooting of Andrew Crawford took place in Parkersburg, West Virginia, in mid-August 1903, when officers and a crowd pursued Crawford, a Black hotel porter, and he was shot in the back. He was accused of threatening a hotel clerk with a revolver and of wounding Special Constable Perry Nolan, and the papers named different men as his shooter.

Crawford had been a porter at the Commercial hotel. The Ceredo Advance said he had quit and drew a gun when the clerk would not pay his wages; the West Virginia News of Ronceverte said he tried to "hold up a hotel clerk" and was paid some money.

Crawford and Nolan exchanged shots in the hotel without effect, and a running fight followed through the streets. Nolan, Constable Jack Helmick and "a large crowd of excited citizens" chased him to a small house at the lower end of the city. Nolan was shot in the foot, either after felling Crawford with his fist or when Crawford pressed a revolver to his side, and Crawford was then shot through the body.

Crawford was taken to the police station and then home in serious condition; the Ronceverte paper reported him paralyzed on one side and "probable he will die." The Ceredo Advance said Nolan would be a cripple for life and that the man who fired the final shot gave bond. No later report of a hearing, a charge against Crawford, or his death appears in the coverage.

The West Virginia News printed the earliest report on August 15 under "Batiled With Police," and the Moorefield Weekly Examiner condensed the same text on August 20. The Ceredo Advance gave the fullest account on August 19 in "State Odds and Ends," calling Crawford "the Negro" throughout. All three white weeklies told the story from the officers' side, and no Black-press report has been found.
The Ronceverte and Moorefield items named Special Policeman A. G. Davis as the shooter. The Ceredo Advance said a young "stranger of Martetta" [Marietta] fired "by order of an officer near by."

reader.title: Shooting of Andrew Crawford
bases: Crawford was shot during a pursuit and arrest by constables and police, by Special Policeman A. G. Davis in one version (A1, A3) and by a civilian acting on an officer's order in another (A2).

Two separately written accounts (A1, with its condensed reprint A3, and A2) agree that the Black porter Crawford drew a revolver at a Parkersburg hotel, fought with Constable Perry Nolan and was shot in the back during his capture.

accounts.label: State-news wire (Ronceverte/Moorefield text)
accounts.gist: Crawford tried to hold up the clerk, was paid some money and left; in a running fight he put his revolver against Nolan's side and shot him in the foot, and Special Policeman Davis shot him in the back, paralyzing one side.

accounts.label: Ceredo Advance version
accounts.gist: Crawford, who had quit as porter, demanded his wages and drew a gun; after a chase with a crowd, Nolan knocked him down, Crawford shot Nolan's foot, and a young stranger shot Crawford by an officer's order.

framing.detail: Headline 'Batiled With Police'; Crawford cast as a would-be robber who fired on officers; his shooting reported without comment.
Opens 'Excitement reigned on the street at Parkersburg'; calls Crawford 'the Negro' throughout and presents the officers' account as fact.
Condensed state-news item in 'West Virginia State Happenings' using 'the negro'.

versions.value: Attempted hold-up of a hotel clerk at revolver point; Crawford was paid some money
Crawford had quit as porter and drew a gun when the clerk would not pay his wages

conflicts.note: Both versions come from the officers' and hotel's side; neither is from a Parkersburg paper.

versions.value: A young stranger from 'Martetta' [Marietta], by order of an officer near by

conflicts.note: A3 condenses A1's text, so the Davis version rests on one source; A2's detail that the shooter gave bond fits a private person, but the coverage does not settle the point.

versions.value: Crawford placed his revolver against Nolan's side and fired; the shot hit Nolan's foot
Crawford fired while down after Nolan felled him with his fist, hitting Nolan's right foot
Paralyzed on one side; 'probable he will die'

conflicts.note: No later report of his death or recovery was found.

Then special policeman A. G. Davis fired, hitting the man in the back, paralyzing one side.
It is probable he will die.

At this point a young man, a stranger of Martetta, pulled a gun and, by order of an officer near by, shot the Negro through the body.
The young man who fired the final shot gave bond for his appearance.
